text: hey everybody winter is coming which means so are all the posts insisting that Christians stole December 25th and
the celebration of Christmas from pagans which is not supported by the data the current scholarly consensus holds that
Christians had calculated December 25th as the date of Jesus's birth as early as around 210 CE and this calculation was
done using an existing tradition that held that prominent historical figures died on the same day of the year as they
were born we see folks like hippolytus around this time period suggesting however that rather than corresponding
to the date of his birth the date of Jesus's death which had traditionally been identified as March 25th corresponded to the date of his
conception and based on a traditional gestational period nine months later we get Jesus being born on December 25th
now this does correspond with the traditional observance of the winter solstice within the Roman Empire at this time and this was not lost on Christians
who would later comment that it only seemed fitting that these significant cosmological events correspond to the
birth of the Savior but we don't have any data that indicate that this inspired the calculation of Jesus's birth on December 25th now the
celebration of Soul Invictus on December 25th would not reach Rome until the late 3rd Century CE uh several decades after
the date of Jesus birth had already been calculated by Christians saturnalia was not celebrated on December 25th it's not
a celebration of the winter solstice it's a harvest celebration and it took place on December 17th and usually ran for a day or two but sometimes as long
as a full week so saturnalia does not actually correspond with the date of Christmas now it did most likely
influence the celebration of Christmas and was most likely helpful in Christmas achieving a place of prominence on the
Christian calendar and so it is not unlikely that things like revelry and gift-giving were borrowed from the celebration of saturnalia now Christmas
is celebrated in many different ways in different parts of the world but there's also a good case to make that within
Europe in the Middle Ages and into the early modern period you had adaptations of pagan celebrations making their way
into the celebration of Christmas in large part because of conversion by large societies whether by force or
otherwise to Christianity and so things like bringing wreaths into the home and decorating and hanging them and
activities associated with the concept of yule and other things like that likely were borrowings from paganism but things like the Christmas tree don't
show any indication of having been borrowed from paganism that seems to be a uniquely Christian Innovation that took place in the late 15th century
within Germany and so there are lots of ways that paganism has influenced the celebration of Christmas particularly in
societies descended from medieval Europe but the notion that the holiday and its date were stolen wholesale from
pre-existing Pagan tradition is just not supported by the data
